title.en: Suan's Good Luck: The Guesser Who Married the Princess
title.zh: 蘇安的好運氣：說中一切的賭徒

region.en: Laguna province, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1a 'Suan's Good Luck', eBook #8299

summary.en: Lazy Suan, ridiculed for leaving school, pretends to be a diviner and 'guesses' what his mother cooks after spying on her. Hiding his father's plough and then 'finding' it, he wins a reputation as a prophet, beats rival datus' riddles by scoffing 'Nonsense!', survives the search for the princess's lost ring when his own cry of despair makes the guilty coachman confess, and marries the princess — every fortune falling to him by accident.
summary.zh: 輟學的懶漢蘇安佯稱通靈，先偷窺母親煮飯而『猜中』晚餐，再藏起父親的犁又『尋回』，博得神算之名。他以一句『胡說』贏過對賭的達圖；公主戒指失竊時，他一句絕望的哀嘆竟令真正的竊賊自首。他因此娶得公主——一切好運皆因巧合而降。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Laguna narrator; archival record. The Juan/Suan cycle of the lucky anti-hero; Fansler notes its kinship with Grimm's 'Dr. Knowall' and Oriental king-wager tales.

passages.text: Suan left school because the other pupils mocked his pronunciation, and went home telling his mother to buy him a pencil and pad of paper, saying he was now the wisest boy in the town. That night he hid his father's plough in a creek near the house; when the plough could not be found next morning, Suan wrote figures of various shapes on the paper and chanted a rhyme that 'meant' the plough had been stolen by a neighbor and hidden in a creek. The father found it there, and in great wonder declared his son truly the wisest boy in town. Later, when Suan's uncle lost his carabao, the same performance traced it to the mountains, and the story of the good guesser spread.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan's Good Luck'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When a royal proclamation promised the princess's hand to whoever could name the thief of her lost ring — death to the one who failed — Suan's mother volunteered him. In the king's carriage Suan despaired aloud, 'Death is at hand!' — and the coachman, who was the real thief, believed himself discovered and knelt begging mercy. Suan shrewdly directed him to hide the ring inside one of the king's geese. The next day, with candle and Latin words, Suan 'divined' that the ring had been swallowed by a goose; the geese were killed and the ring found, and he married the princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan's Good Luck'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A rich datu then came to test the king's famous son-in-law with a golden ball whose contents no one could know, staking his wealth; Suan answered scornfully, 'Nonsense!' — and a bystander shouted that the ball contained nine cents, so Suan won fourteen cascos full of gold, and nobody doubted his merit again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan's Good Luck'; not verbatim.

title.en: Suan Eket and the Ring in the Goose
title.zh: 蘇安·埃凱特與鵝腹之戒

region.en: Rizal province, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home province)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋黎薩省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1b 'Suan Eket', eBook #8299

summary.en: Nicknamed 'Eket' for his inability to say the letter x, Suan quits school declaring himself the wisest boy in town. He 'divines' the plough he has hidden, then his uncle's carabao, and when the princess's ring is lost his despairing cry terrifies the thieving coachman into confessing; Suan orders the ring fed to a goose and divines it there. He wins a melon-seed contest by eavesdropping on the rival king's sailors in a floating tub, and is crowned heir when he smashes the dung-filled bottle crying 'I consider that you are all waste to me.'
summary.zh: 蘇安因發不清x音被喚作『埃凱特』，輟學自稱全鎮最聰明。他以紙上畫符『神算』尋回自藏的犁、舅舅的水牛；公主戒指失竊，他一聲絕望哀嘆嚇得竊賊馬夫自首，他遂令馬夫以鵝吞戒，次日『算』出戒在鵝腹。後又乘木盆漂海偷聽敵王艙中對話而贏瓜籽之賭；最後擲碎糞瓶喊『你們全是我眼中的廢物』——言中瓶中穢物，被加冕為儲君。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Rizal narrator; archival record. Second variant of the lucky-guesser cycle (Tale 1).

passages.text: While studying in a private school Suan could not pronounce the letter x well — he called it 'eket' — so his schoolmates nicknamed him Suan Eket, and he left school, telling his mother to buy him a pencil and pad, for he was now the wisest boy in the town. One night he stole his father's plough and hid it in a creek; the next morning he wrote figures of various shapes on his paper, chanted 'Ararokes, ararokes, Na na nakawes, Ay na s'imburnales' — meaning the plough had been stolen by a neighbor and hidden in a creek — and when his father found it there he declared his son truly wise. The same trick with his uncle Pedro's carabao sent the whole town marveling at the good guesser.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan Eket'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the king's proclamation was read: the princess's ring was lost, and whoever could tell who stole it should have the king's daughter for his wife, while he who tried and failed would lose his head. Suan's mother boasted of her son, and the royal carriage came. In great sorrow Suan said aloud, 'Death is at hand! You will lose your life now' — and the coachman, who had himself stolen the ring, thought he was discovered. He knelt and begged pity; Suan bade him catch one of the king's geese that night and make it swallow the ring. Before the king Suan demanded a candle, went round a round table uttering Latin words, and concluded that the ring, not stolen, had been swallowed by a goose; the geese were killed, the ring found, and the wedding celebrated.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan Eket'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A rich foreign king, Mayabong, then challenged the King of Campao to a wager on melon seeds. Unable to guess, Suan rowed out to sea in a tub intending to drown himself where no one would find his body — but he drifted to Mayabong's casco and overheard the sailors counting the seeds of the green and yellow melons. He answered 'Five' and 'Six' and won the casco of gold. When Mayabong returned with a tightly covered bottle and a second wager, Suan, refusing at first, was compelled by his father-in-law; in rage he hurled the bottle down crying, 'I consider that you are all waste to me' — and the broken bottle proved to contain waste. In great joy the king crowned Suan to succeed him, and he lived happily with his wife the princess.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 1 'Suan Eket'; not verbatim.

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 2 'The Charcoal-Maker who became King', eBook #8299

summary.en: A charcoal-maker's son wins the princess and crown by filling ten cars a day with silver from a magic purse; the princess drugs him and steals the purse. Fleeing, he eats fruit that sprouts horns on his forehead, then fruit that removes them, and returns unrecognized as a palace cook's helper. When the king's household grows horns from the contaminated food, the disguised 'doctor' cures the royal family — with whippings for the king and queen, a dance for the princess, and the condition of his stolen purse returned — marries her, and rules so wisely that the kingdom prospers.
summary.zh: 炭夫之子以神囊連續十日運銀十車，贏得公主與王位；公主灌醉他竊走錢囊。亡命途中，他誤食生角之果，又食脫角之果，遂扮作御廚幫工返宮。王室因毒食長角，他假扮醫師施治——鞭笞國王王后、與公主共舞——換回神囊，娶公主為妻；他雖出身寒微、不學無文，卻禮賢下士，國家因之大治。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Manila narrator; archival record. Fansler places it in Aarne's 'Three Magic Articles and the Wonderful Fruit' cycle.

passages.text: A king proclaimed that whoever could bring him ten car-loads of money for ten successive days should have his beautiful daughter and his crown, on pain of death for failure. The only son of a poor charcoal-maker heard the announcement and told his mother he would marry the princess and be king. Cutting a huge tree in the forest, he heard a voice say, 'Cut this tree no more. Dip your hand into the hole of the trunk, and you will find a purse which will give you all the money you wish.' He found the purse empty at first, but when he angrily threw it down, silver money rolled merrily out of it, and the stream of dollars seemed inexhaustible when he shook it at home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 2 'The Charcoal-Maker who became King'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The youth filled the ten cars before the astonished guards, and for five days the money flowed. The princess, told by her guard that the purse was magical, entertained him regally and tricked him into sleep, stealing the purse and leaving him alone in the chamber. Doomed to die without fulfilling his contract, he fled the kingdom, ate little on his journey, and at last, starving, ate the fruit of a strange tree — and two horns appeared on his forehead. Another tree's fruit made the horns fall off. Collecting both fruits, unrecognizable after two years' travel, he took service unpaid in the royal kitchen, where he proved such an excellent cook that he did all the palace cooking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 2 'The Charcoal-Maker who became King'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day he ground the horn-producing fruit into the king's food and kept the other kind mixed with water in a jar. The king, queen, and princess, used to golden crowns set with diamonds, were seen at table with sharp ugly horns. The terrified cook was sent for a doctor, and the helper intercepted him, pretending the horns could be removed by himself — testing the food on the cook first, and curing him with the water. Dressed as a doctor of surgery, he promised the king not to unfold the matter to the people, and demanded, in return for one-half the kingdom and the princess's hand, the severest treatment: the king and queen to be whipped until they bled, the princess to dance with the doctor until exhausted.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 2 'The Charcoal-Maker who became King'; not verbatim.

passages.text: While the cruel scourging went nearly to killing the royal couple, the doctor fetched the jar of fruit-water and gave them drink; the horns fell off the king and queen, and from the exhausted princess after her dance. A few days afterwards the king and queen died, and the doctor succeeded to the throne with the princess as his wife — telling her that he was the poor charcoal-maker whose magic purse she had stolen. Though uneducated and unrefined, the new king welcomed all wise men to his palace as counsellors, and his kingdom prospered as it had never done under its previous rulers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 2 'The Charcoal-Maker who became King'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Story of Carancal: The Span-Tall Strongman
title.zh: 卡蘭卡爾傳：一拃高的力士

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 3 'The Story of Carancal', eBook #8299

summary.en: Born a span long after his parents' prayers and prophecies, Carancal grows no taller than four feet but eats more than any man and out-wrestles all boys. Driven by poverty, his father twice tries to kill him — dropping a tree on him, sending him to dive at the net — and twice Carancal returns bearing the tree on his shoulders or a slain alligator. Exiled with a five-yard bolo, he defeats three strongmen in wrestling, burns the man-eating giant in the forest house, hurls the great stone out of sight, and marries off his companions to three princesses, remaining a bachelor and benefactor of three kings.
summary.zh: 夫婦祈禱得子，生下僅一拃長的卡蘭卡爾；他長不過四尺，食量驚人，摔跤無敵。貧困的父親兩度設計殺子——倒樹壓頂、誘其潛水——兩次他都肩扛大樹或手提鱷魚歸來。被逐出家門時，他攜五碼長刀上路，連勝三位力士，火燒林中食人巨魔，一舉甩飛巨石；他把三位同伴許配三國公主，自己終身不娶，為三王之恩人。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Batangas narrator; archival record. Eight Filipino variants of this cycle (Pusong, Cabagboc, Sandapal, Sandangcal, etc.); Fansler connects it to the European 'Strong Hans' and 'John the Bear' cycles and to Beowulf's underwater fight.

passages.text: A couple long married but childless begged God every Sunday for a son, and the town witches foretold that he would be born no longer than a span. After a year the boy was born exactly so, yet stronger than anyone would expect, eating a cavan of rice and twenty-five pounds of meat and fish a day by the time he stood four feet tall. Carancal led the town boys in wrestling. When his family's property was all sold to buy him food, his father resolved to kill him in the forest: he set the falling tree on his son and hurried home — but Carancal came back carrying the big tree on his shoulders, asking why he had been left alone. The second attempt, sending him to dive down and see that the net was sound, ended with the sea turning red and foaming — and Carancal walking in with a big alligator under his arm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 3 'The Story of Carancal'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The discouraged mother finally told him to go earn his own living, and with a bolo five yards long Carancal set out. He challenged the first wanderer, Bugtongpalasan, to wrestle for the right to carry the bolo, and won; he defeated Tunkodbola, who could twist up a tree and hurl it out of sight, the earth trembling and trees uprooting as they wrestled; and Macabuhalbundok, who pushed hills over with a laugh, went down too. All four companions reached a large deserted house in the wood and devoured the food on its table. Three of them went hunting while one cooked — and each cook in turn was seized by a giant who came up the stairs crying 'Ho, bajo tao cainco: I smell a man whom I will eat', tying him to a post with a hair from his head.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 3 'The Story of Carancal'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Carancal's turn came he had his companions shave his head. The giant, seeing the white head, laughed and demanded his own head be made white too; Carancal said heads must be shaved to be white, and it was a very difficult thing to shave a head. The impatient giant insisted, so Carancal tied him tightly to a post with ropes, smeared his body with wax, and set it on fire, destroying him; the four lived in the house as if it were their own. Then came the king's letter: a huge stone covered much ground in a kingdom across the sea, and its removal won the hand of the prettiest princess. After three weeks' swimming — discovering that the island they rested on was really a very big fish, which fortunately carried them near the kingdom — Carancal swung the great stone out of sight with one pull, and married one of his companions, Bugtongpalasan, to the princess instead of himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 3 'The Story of Carancal'; not verbatim.

passages.text: King Walangtacut next begged them to drag a monstrous decaying fish from his shore, and again only Carancal succeeded, marrying Tunkodbola to that princess in his place. A third king's letter told of a stone so big 'I thought it was the sky that fell'; Carancal moved it again, and Macabuhalbundok was married off. The three princes considered Carancal their father though he was younger than any of them, and as their fathers-in-law died one by one, all three became kings. Carancal at last visited his cruel parents with plenty of money, and lived once more with them, with three kings under him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 3 'The Story of Carancal'; not verbatim.

title.en: Suac and His Adventures: The Boy Who Killed Pugut
title.zh: 蘇瓦克歷險：誅殺普古特的少年

region.en: Arayat, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省阿拉亞特（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Pampangan oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4a 'Suac and his Adventures', eBook #8299

summary.en: Three young hunters on Mt. Telapayong lose each meal to Pugut, the huge black man in the tree who eats what is cooked beneath him. When Suac's turn comes to cook, he pushes the bearded ogre into the fire, lures him over a grass-covered pit, and finally shoves him into a crocodile's mouth. Taking Pugut's club, Suac kills the nightly man-eating giant of the town and then rids the islands of all wild monsters, becoming ruler over his people.
summary.zh: 三名少年獵人在特拉帕永山烹食，屢被樹上黑巨人普古特搶食。輪到蘇瓦克掌炊時，他先將普古特推入火中燒鬈其鬚，再誘其踏入草掩之陷阱，最後將其推入鱷口誅之。蘇瓦克持普古特之棒擊斃夜裡食人的巨人，繼而清除諸島所有野獸妖魔，成為族人之王。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan folktale recorded by Fansler from an Arayat narrator; archival record. The 'interrupted-cooking' ogre episode of the John the Bear cycle.

passages.text: In a certain town in Pampanga lived a boy named Suac, who went hunting with Sunga and Sacu on Mount Telapayong to try his fortune. Having caught a large hog, they left Sacu to cook under a large tree while the others hunted — and a horrible creature, a very large black man with a long beard named Pugut, called down from the treetop, 'Ha, ha! What a nice meal you are preparing! Hurry up! I am hungry.' Sacu resisted, but Pugut knocked him down and ate all the food; the same happened when Sunga cooked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4 'Suac and his Adventures'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Suac was left to cook and roast the hog, Pugut threatened to eat him up along with the food. Suac placed the food near the fire, stood by it, and when Pugut tried to seize it, pushed him into the fire; Pugut's beard was burnt and became kinky. The boy ran to a deep pit, covered it with grass, and stood on the opposite side crying, 'I pray you, do not step on my grass!' Pugut stepped on the grass and fell into the pit, but Suac had not gone far when the ogre was following him again — until Suac, seeing a crocodile, waited resolutely, gave him a blow, and pushed him into the mouth of the crocodile. Thus Pugut was destroyed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4 'Suac and his Adventures'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Suac took his victim's club, and when he heard that a giant came every night into the neighborhood to devour people, he went to encounter him; one deadly blow of Pugut's club tumbled the giant down dead. Later Suac rid the islands of all the wild monsters, and became the ruler over his people.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4 'Suac and his Adventures'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Friends, the Monkey, the Dog, and the Carabao: Against the Buñgisñgis

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4b 'The Three Friends — the Monkey, the Dog, and the Carabao', eBook #8299

summary.en: Three animal friends hunting in the country lose their meals one by one to the Buñgisñgis, who throws the carabao knee-deep into the earth and bullies the dog; the monkey alone sets a pitfall before cooking and buries the ogre. His foolish companions dig the ogre up and are killed and lamed; the monkey survives, cheats the Buñgisñgis into stirring a beehive and wearing a boa as a belt, and leads him to his death on a crocodile.
summary.zh: 猴、狗、水牛三友鄉間行獵，輪流掌炊；班吉斯尼巨人連連搶食，把水牛扔得膝陷入土，欺凌狗兒。唯有猴子先掘陷阱，禮讓巨人入座，一拉椅腿將其活埋。愚蠢的夥伴們挖開墳墓，反遭巨人殺死弄殘；猴子誘其去搖蜂窩『報時』、以蟒蛇作腰帶，終將其引至鱷口喪命。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Batangas narrator; archival record. The Buñgisñgis is the Tagalog one-eyed ogre; this is the animal-companion form of the interrupted-cooking episode.

passages.text: Once there lived three friends — a monkey, a dog, and a carabao — who, tired of city life, went to the country to hunt with rice, meat, and kitchen utensils. The first day the carabao cooked while the others hunted; the noise of frying was heard by the Buñgisñgis in the forest, who came saying, 'Well, friend, I see that you have prepared food for me.' The carabao made a furious attack, but the Buñgisñgis seized him by the horn and threw him knee-deep into the earth, then ate up all the food and disappeared. The next day the dog was cook and could only retire to a corner and watch his unwelcome guest eat; the third day the monkey was cook.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4 'The Three Friends'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before cooking, the monkey made a pitfall in front of the stove, put away enough food for his companions and himself, and set the rice on the stove. When the Buñgisñgis came, he said very politely, 'Sir, you have come just in time. The food is ready, and I hope you'll compliment me by accepting it.' As the ogre sat down in a chair and devoured the food, the monkey took hold of a leg of the chair, gave a jerk, and sent his guest tumbling into the pit, filling it with earth so that the Buñgisñgis was buried with no solemnity. But the foolish companions, curious, dug up the grave; the Buñgisñgis jumped out still alive, killed the dog and lamed the carabao, while the monkey escaped up a tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4 'The Three Friends'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Wandering in the forest, the monkey found a beehive on top of a vine, and when the Buñgisñgis came to kill him he pleaded for his life, saying the king had appointed him to ring each hour of the day the bell up there. The delighted ogre accepted the position and, after waiting long, pulled the vine — and the bees buzzed about him and punished his curiosity. Maddened with pain, he found the monkey playing with a boa-constrictor and swore to kill him; the monkey offered his beautiful belt, 'which the king has given me' — and led him, wearing the living snake, to his final destruction on a crocodile.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 4 'The Three Friends'; not verbatim.
